title: Kubernetes Core Concepts
summary: Kubernetes is the de facto standard for running containerized workloads in production. Understanding its architecture and core objects — Pods, Deployments, Services, and Namespaces — is the foundation for everything from debugging to GitOps.

sections.title: Architecture: control plane and worker nodes
sections.body:
Kubernetes is a distributed system that manages containerized applications across a cluster of machines.

```
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  CONTROL PLANE                    │
│                                                   │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  │
│  │   API    │  │           │  │               │  │
│  │  Server  │  │  etcd     │  │  Scheduler    │  │
│  │(kubectl  │  │(key-value │  │(places pods   │  │
│  │ talks to)│  │ store)    │  │ on nodes)     │  │
│  └──────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────────┘  │
│                  ┌─────────────────────────────┐  │
│                  │  Controller Manager          │  │
│                  │  (reconciles desired state)  │  │
│                  └─────────────────────────────┘  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
             │ watches/manages
┌────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  WORKER NODES                     │
│                                                   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Node 1                                   │    │
│  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌────────┐  │    │
│  │  │  kubelet │  │kube-proxy │  │  Pod   │  │    │
│  │  │(runs pods│  │(iptables) │  │[cont1] │  │    │
│  │  │ on node) │  │           │  │[cont2] │  │    │
│  │  └──────────┘  └───────────┘  └────────┘  │    │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key components:**
- **API Server**: all communication goes through this — kubectl, controllers, kubelet
- **etcd**: distributed key-value store — the ground truth for cluster state
- **Scheduler**: decides which node a new pod runs on (based on resources, affinity, taints)
- **Controller Manager**: runs controllers that watch state and reconcile (deployment controller, replicaset controller, etc.)
- **kubelet**: agent on each worker node, runs containers via the container runtime
- **kube-proxy**: maintains iptables rules for Service routing

```bash
# In the sandbox (k3s is a lightweight single-node Kubernetes)
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get nodes -o wide      # shows OS, container runtime, IP
kubectl describe node <name>   # full node info: capacity, conditions, pods

# Check control plane components
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```

sections.title: Pods, ReplicaSets, and Deployments
sections.body:
These three objects form a hierarchy. You almost always create Deployments, not Pods directly.

**Pod** — the smallest deployable unit. Contains one or more containers that share network and storage.

```yaml
# A bare pod (rarely used directly in production)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-app
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25-alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: 64Mi
      limits:
        memory: 128Mi
```

**Deployment** — manages a ReplicaSet (maintains N copies of your pod). Handles rolling updates and rollbacks.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app         # must match pod template labels
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # allow 1 extra pod during update
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never go below desired replicas
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 50m
            memory: 64Mi
          limits:
            memory: 128Mi
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
```

```bash
# Explore the existing sandbox deployments
kubectl get deployments -A
kubectl describe deployment web-app -n default
kubectl get replicasets -n default

# Scale
kubectl scale deployment web-app --replicas=5 -n default

# Rolling restart (triggers new rollout without changing image)
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-app -n default

# Watch rollout status
kubectl rollout status deployment/web-app -n default

# Rollback if something breaks
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app -n default
kubectl rollout history deployment/web-app -n default
```

sections.title: Services: stable network endpoints for pods
sections.body:
Pods are ephemeral — they get new IPs every time they restart. A Service provides a stable DNS name and IP that routes to healthy pods.

```yaml
# ClusterIP (default) — internal cluster access only
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: default
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web-app         # routes to pods with this label
  ports:
  - port: 80             # service port (what you access)
    targetPort: 80       # pod port (what the container listens on)
    protocol: TCP
```

**Service types:**

```yaml
# NodePort — expose on every node's IP at a port 30000-32767
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 30080   # optional; auto-assigned if omitted

# LoadBalancer — provision cloud LB (on AWS: creates ELB)
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
  - port: 443
    targetPort: 8080
```

```bash
# Services in the sandbox
kubectl get svc -A                     # all services
kubectl get svc -n argocd              # ArgoCD services
kubectl describe svc web-app           # endpoints, selector, ports

# Port-forward: access a service from your local machine
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:80 &
# Now: curl http://localhost:8080

# Endpoints: what pods the service routes to
kubectl get endpoints web-app
kubectl get endpoints argocd-server -n argocd

# DNS: services are reachable inside the cluster at:
# <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
# kubectl exec a pod to test:
kubectl exec -n default deploy/web-app -- \
  wget -qO- http://web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
```

sections.title: Namespaces, labels, and resource organization
sections.body:
**Namespaces** provide logical isolation within a cluster. They're used to separate environments (dev/staging), teams, or application groups.

```bash
# Sandbox namespaces
kubectl get namespaces
# NAME              STATUS
# default           Active    ← general workloads
# kube-system       Active    ← Kubernetes system components
# argocd            Active    ← ArgoCD GitOps
# monitoring        Active    ← Prometheus, Grafana
# learning          Active    ← exercise workloads
# external-secrets  Active    ← ESO operator

# Create a namespace
kubectl create namespace staging

# Namespace-scoped commands
kubectl get pods -n argocd
kubectl get all -n monitoring

# Set default namespace for your context (saves typing -n every time)
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=argocd
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default  # reset
```

**Labels** are key-value pairs attached to any resource. They're used for selection (by Services, Deployments, monitoring), filtering, and organization.

```bash
# View labels
kubectl get pods --show-labels
kubectl get pods -l app=web-app         # filter by label
kubectl get pods -l 'app in (web-app,broken-app)'  # multiple values

# Label a resource
kubectl label pod my-pod environment=staging
kubectl label pod my-pod environment-  # remove a label

# Annotations: non-identifying metadata (not used for selection)
kubectl annotate deployment web-app \
  deployed-by=esteban \
  last-deploy=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

# Common label conventions (follow these in your own workloads)
# app.kubernetes.io/name: web-app
# app.kubernetes.io/version: v1.2.3
# app.kubernetes.io/component: frontend
# app.kubernetes.io/part-of: my-platform
# app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: argocd
```

sections.title: Exercise: deploy and operate a workload
sections.body:
Deploy a new application to the sandbox cluster and practice the full operational lifecycle.

```bash
# 1. Deploy an app
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: demo-app
  namespace: learning
  labels:
    app: demo-app
    version: v1.0.0
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: demo
        image: hashicorp/http-echo:1.0
        args: ["-text=hello from demo-app", "-listen=:5678"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 10m
            memory: 16Mi
          limits:
            memory: 32Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: demo-app
  namespace: learning
spec:
  selector:
    app: demo-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 5678
EOF

# 2. Watch it come up
kubectl rollout status deployment/demo-app -n learning

# 3. Test it
kubectl port-forward svc/demo-app -n learning 8090:80 &
curl http://localhost:8090

# 4. Scale it
kubectl scale deployment demo-app --replicas=4 -n learning
kubectl get pods -n learning -l app=demo-app

# 5. Trigger a rolling update (change the message)
kubectl set env deployment/demo-app -n learning NEW_MESSAGE=v2
kubectl rollout status deployment/demo-app -n learning

# 6. Roll back
kubectl rollout undo deployment/demo-app -n learning

# 7. Clean up
kubectl delete deployment demo-app -n learning
kubectl delete svc demo-app -n learning
```
